title: The projective dimension of the residue field is at least dim m/m^2
statement: Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] with residue field $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$, and let $n=\dim_\kappa\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ (finite, as $\mathfrak m$ is finitely generated). If $\kappa$, as an $R$-module, has a projective resolution $0\to P_d\to\dots\to P_0\to\kappa\to0$ of length $\le d$ [def-weil-pbc-finite-global-dimension] for an integer $d\ge0$, then $d\ge n$. Equivalently: $\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa\ge\dim_\kappa\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00OA (lemma-length-resolution-residue-field, line 26966), with its proof (Koszul complex on a lift of a basis of m/m^2, minimal finite free resolution via Lemmas what-kind-of-resolutions-Noetherian-local and add-trivial-complex, comparison map by Lemma compare-resolutions, induction on the injectivity of alpha_i tensor kappa). Tag verified in tags/tags: 00OA,algebra-lemma-length-resolution-residue-field

proof.text: (Choice of $x_1,\dots,x_n$.) As $R$ is Noetherian, $\mathfrak m$ is a finitely generated $R$-module, so $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ is a finitely generated module over $R/\mathfrak m=\kappa$, i.e. a finite dimensional $\kappa$-vector space; $n$ is its dimension. Choose $x_1,\dots,x_n\in\mathfrak m$ whose classes $\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_n$ form a $\kappa$-basis of $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$. Let $0\to P_d\to\cdots\to P_0\to\kappa\to0$ be the given projective resolution, $d\ge0$. If $n=0$ then $d\ge0=n$ and there is nothing to prove; the following steps work for every $n\ge0$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00OA (lemma-length-resolution-residue-field), line 26975: 'Let x_1,...,x_n be elements of m whose images in m/m^2 form a basis'

proof.text: (The Koszul complex.) For $0\le i\le n$ let $K_i$ be the free $R$-module [def-weil-pbc-free-module] with basis $e_J$, $J$ running over the subsets $J=\{j_1<\dots<j_i\}$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with $i$ elements (this is $\wedge^iR^n$, with $e_J=e_{j_1}\wedge\dots\wedge e_{j_i}$); $K_0=R$ with basis $e_\emptyset=1$, and $K_i=0$ for $i>n$. For $i\ge1$ let $d_i:K_i\to K_{i-1}$ be the $R$-linear map with $$d_i(e_J)=\sum_{a=1}^{i}(-1)^{a+1}x_{j_a}\,e_{J\setminus\{j_a\}}.$$ Then $d_{i-1}\circ d_i=0$ for $i\ge2$: for $a<b$ the basis vector $e_{J\setminus\{j_a,j_b\}}$ arises in $d_{i-1}d_i(e_J)$ twice, by removing $j_a$ first (sign $(-1)^{a+1}$) and then $j_b$, which is now in position $b-1$ (sign $(-1)^{b}$), and by removing $j_b$ first (sign $(-1)^{b+1}$) and then $j_a$, still in position $a$ (sign $(-1)^{a+1}$); the two terms are $\pm x_{j_a}x_{j_b}e_{J\setminus\{j_a,j_b\}}$ with signs $(-1)^{a+b+1}$ and $(-1)^{a+b}$, and cancel. Let $\pi:K_0=R\to\kappa$ be the quotient map; $\pi\circ d_1=0$ because $\pi(d_1(e_{\{j\}}))=\pi(x_j)=0$ as $x_j\in\mathfrak m$. So $\cdots\to K_1\xrightarrow{d_1}K_0\xrightarrow{\pi}\kappa$ is a complex of free $R$-modules over $\kappa$ (it need not be exact). Moreover, since every coefficient $\pm x_{j_a}$ lies in $\mathfrak m$, $d_i(K_i)\subseteq\mathfrak mK_{i-1}$ for all $i\ge1$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00OA (lemma-length-resolution-residue-field), lines 26976--26990 (definition of K(R,x); 'It is easy to see that this is a complex'); the remark there that the cokernel of K_1 -> K_0 is kappa by Lemma 00DV (8) is not used below: only pi o d_1 = 0 is needed

proof.text: (Minimal finite free resolution.) $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$ is a finitely generated $R$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module] (generated by the class of $1$) and has a projective resolution of length $\le d$ [def-weil-pbc-finite-global-dimension]. By [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-finite-free-resolution-local] there is an exact sequence [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence] $0\to F_d\xrightarrow{\varphi_d}\cdots\xrightarrow{\varphi_1}F_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}\kappa\to0$ with every $F_i$ finite free and $\varphi_i(F_i)\subseteq\mathfrak mF_{i-1}$ for $1\le i\le d$. Put $F_i=0$ and $\varphi_i=0$ for $i>d$; the sequence $\cdots\to F_1\to F_0\to\kappa\to0$ stays exact (exactness at $F_d$ is the injectivity of $\varphi_d$) and $\varphi_i(F_i)\subseteq\mathfrak mF_{i-1}$ now holds for all $i\ge1$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00OA (lemma-length-resolution-residue-field), lines 26989--26996 (Lemmas 0CXF what-kind-of-resolutions-Noetherian-local and 00MT add-trivial-complex)

proof.text: (Comparison map.) Apply [lem-weil-pbc-free-complex-maps-to-resolution] with $M=N=\kappa$, $\varphi=\mathrm{id}_\kappa$, the complex of free modules $(K_\bullet,d_\bullet,\pi)$ over $\kappa$ of Step 2 and the resolution $(F_\bullet,\varphi_\bullet,\varepsilon)$ of $\kappa$ of Step 3. It gives $R$-linear maps $\alpha_i:K_i\to F_i$ ($i\ge0$) with $\varepsilon\circ\alpha_0=\pi$ and $\varphi_i\circ\alpha_i=\alpha_{i-1}\circ d_i$ for $i\ge1$.

proof.text:
(Reduction mod $\mathfrak m$; notation.) For an $R$-module $G$ write $ ar G=G/\mathfrak mG$ ($=G\otimes_R\kappa$, a $\kappa$-vector space) and, for an $R$-linear $f:G	o G'$, $ ar f: ar G	o ar G'$ for the induced map. Let $G$ be a finite free $R$-module [def-weil-pbc-free-module] with basis $g_1,\dots,g_k$. (a) The map $	heta_G: ar G^{\oplus n}	o\mathfrak mG/\mathfrak m^2G$, $( ar y_1,\dots, ar y_n)\mapsto[\sum_jx_jy_j]$, is well defined (changing $y_j$ by an element of $\mathfrak mG$ changes $\sum_jx_jy_j$ by an element of $\mathfrak m^2G$) and is an isomorphism of $\kappa$-vector spaces: writing $y_j=\sum_lc_{jl}g_l$, the element $\sum_jx_jy_j=\sum_l(\sum_jc_{jl}x_j)g_l$, and $\mathfrak mG/\mathfrak m^2G\cong(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2)^{\oplus k}$ through the coordinates in the basis $g_l$; since $ ar x_1,\dots, ar x_n$ is a $\kappa$-basis of $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$, every coordinate vector arises from exactly one family $( ar c_{jl})$ of residues. (b) If $f:G	o G'$ is $R$-linear between finite free modules, then $f(\mathfrak mG)\subseteq\mathfrak mG'$ and $f(\mathfrak m^2G)\subseteq\mathfrak m^2G'$, so $f$ induces $f^
atural:\mathfrak mG/\mathfrak m^2G	o\mathfrak mG'/\mathfrak m^2G'$, and $f^
atural\circ	heta_G=	heta_{G'}\circ ar f^{\oplus n}$ (both send $( ar y_j)_j$ to $[\sum_jx_jf(y_j)]$). Hence if $ ar f$ is injective, so are $ ar f^{\oplus n}$ and $f^
atural=	heta_{G'}\circ ar f^{\oplus n}\circ	heta_G^{-1}$. (c) If $g:G	o G'$ is $R$-linear with $g(G)\subseteq\mathfrak mG'$, then $\hat g: ar G	o\mathfrak mG'/\mathfrak m^2G'$, $ ar y\mapsto[g(y)]$, is well defined, since $g(\mathfrak mG)=\mathfrak m\,g(G)\subseteq\mathfrak m^2G'$.

proof.text:
(The commutative square.) Let $i\ge1$. By Step 2 and Step 3, $d_i(K_i)\subseteq\mathfrak mK_{i-1}$ and $\varphi_i(F_i)\subseteq\mathfrak mF_{i-1}$, so Step 5 (c) gives $\hat d_i: ar K_i	o\mathfrak mK_{i-1}/\mathfrak m^2K_{i-1}$ and $\hat\varphi_i: ar F_i	o\mathfrak mF_{i-1}/\mathfrak m^2F_{i-1}$, and Step 5 (b) gives $\alpha_{i-1}^
atural$. For $y\in K_i$, $\hat\varphi_i( ar\alpha_i( ar y))=[\varphi_i\alpha_i(y)]=[\alpha_{i-1}d_i(y)]=\alpha_{i-1}^
atural(\hat d_i( ar y))$ by Step 4. Hence $\hat\varphi_i\circ ar\alpha_i=\alpha_{i-1}^
atural\circ\hat d_i$.

proof.text:
($\hat d_i$ is injective, 'by hand'.) Let $1\le i\le n$ (for $i>n$, $ ar K_i=0$). $ ar K_i$ and $ ar K_{i-1}$ have the $\kappa$-bases $ ar e_J$ (Step 5 (a) applied to the bases of Step 2). By the formula of Step 2, $	heta_{K_{i-1}}^{-1}\hat d_i( ar e_J)=(c_1,\dots,c_n)\in ar K_{i-1}^{\oplus n}$ with $c_j=(-1)^{a+1} ar e_{J\setminus\{j\}}$ if $j=j_a\in J$ and $c_j=0$ if $j
otin J$. Let $\omega=\sum_J\lambda_J ar e_J$ ($\lambda_J\in\kappa$, $|J|=i$) with $\hat d_i(\omega)=0$. Fix $J$ and let $j\in J$ (possible as $i\ge1$). The $j$-th component of $	heta_{K_{i-1}}^{-1}\hat d_i(\omega)$ is $\sum_{J'
i j}\pm\lambda_{J'} ar e_{J'\setminus\{j\}}$; the sets $J'\setminus\{j\}$ for $J'
i j$ are pairwise distinct (as $J'=(J'\setminus\{j\})\cup\{j\}$), so the coefficient of the basis vector $ ar e_{J\setminus\{j\}}$ in it is $\pm\lambda_J$, and it vanishes. Hence all $\lambda_J=0$ and $\omega=0$: $\hat d_i$ is injective.

proof.text: (Induction: $\bar\alpha_i$ is injective for all $i\ge0$.) Case $i=0$: $\varepsilon$ induces $\bar\varepsilon:\bar F_0\to\kappa/\mathfrak m\kappa=\kappa$ and $\pi$ induces $\bar\pi=\mathrm{id}:\bar K_0=R/\mathfrak m\to\kappa$; from $\varepsilon\circ\alpha_0=\pi$ (Step 4), $\bar\varepsilon\circ\bar\alpha_0=\mathrm{id}_\kappa$, so $\bar\alpha_0$ is injective. Step: let $i\ge1$ and assume $\bar\alpha_{i-1}$ injective. Then $\alpha_{i-1}^\natural$ is injective by Step 5 (b) ($K_{i-1}$, $F_{i-1}$ are finite free), $\hat d_i$ is injective by Step 7, so $\hat\varphi_i\circ\bar\alpha_i=\alpha_{i-1}^\natural\circ\hat d_i$ (Step 6) is injective, and therefore $\bar\alpha_i$ is injective.

e0$, and $ ar\alpha_n: ar K_n	o ar F_n$ is injective by Step 8; hence $ ar F_n
e0$ and $F_n
e0$. Since $F_i=0$ for $i>d$ (Step 3), $n\le d$.
